# Delays are not observed exactly

## Two events, two windows

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- A delay is the time between two events. Infection to symptom onset,
  onset to hospitalisation, onset to death
- Neither event is seen at a point in time. Both arrive as a day,
  sometimes a week
- In real time the data is right truncated as well. Long delays have
  not had time to be observed
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Ignore any of that and the estimate is biased
- The estimate is then used as an input to forecasts and to
  transmission models, which inherit the bias
- Everyone in this field hits the same three adjustments, and most of
  us have written them at least once
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note}
The maths has been settled for years. What follows is about what it
took to make it usable twice, in two languages.
:::

## The adjustment

$$
F_{\mathrm{pc}}(t) \;=\; \int_{0}^{w} F_{d}(t - u)\, f_{p}(u)\,
\mathrm{d}u
$$

- $F_d$ is the delay CDF and $f_p$ the density of when, inside a window
  of width $w$, the primary event happened
- Secondary interval censoring is then a difference of $F_{\mathrm{pc}}$
  across the observation window
- Right truncation divides by $F_{\mathrm{pc}}(D)$
- Three pairs of delay and primary distribution are implemented in
  closed form. Everything else needs the integral

::: {.callout-important}
The whole engineering story is that integral, and the fact that a
sampler has to differentiate through it.
:::
